alignment.note: The Greek imperfect ἔλεγεν ('he was saying') is matched by the Latin imperfect dicebat, both conveying durative or repeated speech; the Syriac ܘܐܡܪ is a simple perfect bundled with the conjunction, lacking the explicit imperfective nuance.

Greek introduces direct discourse with recitative ὅτι followed by a colon; the Vulgate marks the same with a bare colon. The Syriac has no separate particle here, folding the transition directly into the interrogative ܕܠܡܐ.
Interrogative expecting a negative answer: μήτι / ܕܠܡܐ / Numquid.
ὁ λύχνος / ܫܪܓܐ / lucerna ('the lamp'); Syriac and Latin lack the definite article available in Greek but the referent is identical.

Greek purpose conjunction ἵνα is rendered by Latin final ut; the Syriac expresses the same purpose clause without a discrete conjunction, embedding it in the prefixed relative-locative ܕܬܚܝܬ at the next token.
'under the basket': Greek ὑπὸ τὸν μόδιον, Latin sub modio, Syriac ܕܬܚܝܬ ܣܐܬܐ; the Syriac fuses the relative/purpose marker with the preposition in a single prefixed form.
Passive subjunctive 'that it be placed': τεθῇ / ܢܬܬܣܝܡ / ponatur.
'under the bed': ὑπὸ τὴν κλίνην / ܬܚܝܬ ܥܪܣܐ / sub lecto, the three traditions agreeing on the parallel locative.

Greek expresses the rhetorical question with the single negative particle οὐχ, and Latin with nonne; the Syriac uses the two-word negated copula ܠܐ ܗܘܐ ('is it not'), a periphrastic construction yielding the same emphatic positive expectation.
The purpose conjunction ἵνα / ut is repeated in Greek and Latin; the Syriac again has no discrete conjunction, encoding the clause through the prefixed relative ܕܥܠ at the following token.
'upon the lampstand': ἐπὶ τὴν λυχνίαν / ܕܥܠ ܡܢܪܬܐ / super candelabrum; the Syriac ܡܢܪܬܐ derives from the root n-w-r ('light/fire'), the same semantic field as Greek λυχνία (from λύχνος).
Closing passive subjunctive with interrogative force: τεθῇ; / ܢܬܬܣܝܡ / ponatur ?
